title: Biggest Lottery Winners: What Happened After They Won
description: From quitting jobs by phone to wishing they'd torn up the ticket — the true stories of America's biggest lottery winners and what the money really did.
content:
The Night Everything Changed

It almost never looks the way you'd imagine. No fireworks, no crowd, no slow-motion moment of clarity. For most of the biggest lottery winners in American history, the moment of realization happened somewhere ordinary — a gas station, a living room couch, a phone with a cracked screen. The numbers matched. And then life, in every sense they'd previously understood it, was over.

What makes these stories worth telling isn't the amount on the check. It's what happened in the hours, months, and years that followed. The decisions made in a daze. The relationships that shifted. The things money fixed and the things it couldn't touch. These are the stories behind the headlines — and they reveal more about human nature than any dollar figure can.

Section 1: Who Were These People Before the Win

A Hospital Worker, a Retiree, and a Young Man in Wisconsin

Mavis Wanczyk was a 53-year-old hospital worker from Chicopee, Massachusetts, who had spent 32 years working at Mercy Medical Center. She wasn't wealthy. She was, by her own account, a regular person doing a regular job, raising a family, living a life that most people would recognize without much explanation. When she won the $758.7 million Powerball jackpot in August 2017 — the largest single-ticket Powerball win at the time — she was still on her shift.

Gloria MacKenzie was 84 years old in May 2013 when she claimed a $590.5 million Powerball jackpot in Florida, making her the oldest solo jackpot winner in U.S. lottery history. She lived quietly. She wasn't known for public statements or spectacle. She was, in almost every visible way, an ordinary retiree living in Zephyrhills, a small city northeast of Tampa. See Florida lottery information for context on how that state handles major winners.

Manuel Franco was 24 years old when he won a $768.4 million Powerball jackpot in March 2019 in Wisconsin — at the time the third-largest lottery jackpot ever awarded to a single ticket. He was young enough that most of his adult life was still ahead of him. Jack Whittaker, by contrast, was already a successful contractor in West Virginia when he won $314.9 million in Powerball in December 2002. He was worth an estimated $17 million before he ever bought that ticket.

Section 2: The Claim — First Decisions Made in 24 Hours

The Phone Call, the Press Conference, the Wait

The first decision every winner faces is deceptively simple: tell someone, or don't. Mavis Wanczyk made her choice quickly. She called her employer and quit on the spot, right there on the phone. "I just want to be with my family and do what I want to do," she told reporters at a Massachusetts State Lottery press conference the following day. The decision was immediate, instinctive, and — for her — clearly the right one.

Not everyone moved that fast. Merle and Patricia Butler, who shared a $218.6 million piece of the March 2012 Mega Millions jackpot in Illinois, waited months before coming forward to claim their share. Financial advisors and lottery attorneys typically recommend exactly that kind of pause — time to establish legal structures, consult professionals, and make deliberate choices rather than reactive ones. The Butlers appear to have done exactly that.

Among the first decisions winners must make is the one with the most immediate financial impact: lump sum or annuity. The lump sum option delivers a significantly smaller amount upfront — typically around 60% of the advertised jackpot before taxes — while the annuity pays out over 29 years. After federal and state taxes, the difference in take-home wealth can be enormous. Use a lottery tax calculator to understand just how much of an announced jackpot actually reaches the winner's hands.

Section 4: The Longer Story — What the Money Did and Didn't Do

When Everything Goes Right — and When It Doesn't

For some of the biggest lottery winners, the money appears to have done exactly what most people hope it would: it provided security, freedom, and options. Mavis Wanczyk stepped away from her job, stepped into privacy, and largely disappeared from public view — which, depending on your perspective, looks like exactly the right outcome. Manuel Franco, 24 years old and newly worth hundreds of millions, told reporters he planned to "live life to the fullest." The details of what that looked like remained mostly private.

Edwin Castro, who claimed the $2.04 billion Powerball jackpot in November 2022 — the largest lottery jackpot in U.S. history — took the lump sum option, receiving approximately $997.6 million before taxes. He became the first confirmed individual to win a jackpot exceeding $2 billion. Castro was identified publicly in California, a state that requires winner disclosure for jackpots over $1 million, though he initially remained largely out of the public spotlight in the months following his claim.

Jack Whittaker's story is different — and it demands honesty. He was already wealthy when he won. He made significant public donations after his win, including to churches and charities in West Virginia. But the years that followed brought a cascade of documented difficulties: thefts of large amounts of cash from his vehicle, lawsuits, and legal troubles. Most publicly, his granddaughter Brandi, whom he had spoken about caring for in his winner's press conference, died in 2004. In interviews, Whittaker said the win had brought him more grief than happiness. "I wish I'd torn that ticket up," he was reported to have said.

What Winners Typically Did With the Money

  • Took the lump sum payment, accepting a significantly reduced amount upfront
  • Paid substantial federal and state income taxes on their winnings
  • Hired attorneys and financial advisors — often before making any public statement
  • Made donations to churches, charities, and community organizations
  • Supported family members financially
  • In some cases, relocated to protect their privacy

Section 5: The Most Human Moment

"I just want to be with my family and do what I want to do." — Mavis Wanczyk, at her Massachusetts State Lottery press conference, August 2017, the day after winning a $758.7 million Powerball jackpot

It's worth sitting with that quote for a moment. Here was a woman who had just been handed more money than most people could meaningfully visualize — and what she said, in front of cameras and reporters and the full attention of a stunned public, was something that could have come from anyone. Family. Time. Choice. The desire to do what she wanted. It didn't sound like the speech of someone who had won hundreds of millions of dollars. It sounded like someone who had spent 32 years doing a job that wasn't her first choice, and had just been given the rarest of things: a way out.

Section 6: What These Stories Actually Teach Us

The Patterns That Emerge Across Decades of Big Wins

Taken together, the stories of the biggest lottery winners in American history don't add up to a simple lesson. They don't prove that money buys happiness, and they don't prove that it doesn't. What they do reveal, consistently, is that sudden wealth amplifies whatever was already true. For Jack Whittaker, who had money before the win, the jackpot brought scrutiny, opportunists, and grief that his existing wealth couldn't insulate him from. For Mavis Wanczyk, who wanted privacy and simplicity, the win seems to have delivered exactly that.

The practical patterns are worth noting. Winners who waited before claiming — who consulted lawyers, set up trusts, thought through disclosure in states where anonymity was an option — tended to have more control over what happened next. The ones who moved fastest, who made decisions in the first emotional hours, faced more turbulence in the aftermath. That's not a judgment; it's just what the documented record shows.

What the record also shows is that these were, before anything else, ordinary people. A hospital worker. A retiree in a small Florida city. A 24-year-old in Wisconsin. A contractor in West Virginia. They didn't become extraordinary because of the numbers on a ticket. They became, briefly, the most watched ordinary people in the country — and what they did with that attention, and with the money, varied enormously from one to the next.
